subject: chemistry
title: Acids, neutralisation and titrations
key_idea: Acids release H⁺ ions in water and alkalis release OH⁻ ions. Strong acids dissociate fully, weak acids only partly. Neutralisation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, and a titration uses it to find an unknown concentration.

blocks.text: Learn the names and formulae of these acids and alkalis, and the ion each releases.

items.meaning: A substance that releases H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
A water-soluble base that releases OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.

items: Acids release H⁺. Alkalis release OH⁻.
Sulfuric acid can release two H⁺ per molecule.
Learn the formulae of the four acids and three alkalis.

blocks.text: Strength is about how far an acid dissociates, not how concentrated it is.

items.meaning: An acid that is fully dissociated in aqueous solution, e.g. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻.
An acid that is only partially dissociated in aqueous solution, e.g. CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.

items: Strong bases such as NaOH and KOH are fully dissociated. Weak bases such as NH₃ are partially dissociated.
Strength is not concentration. A dilute solution of a strong acid can have fewer H⁺ ions than a concentrated solution of a weak one.

rows: Reaction with a reactive metal such as magnesium

blocks.text: The total amount of gas from the same moles of each acid is the same in the end, because the weak acid keeps dissociating as H⁺ is used up.

items: Strong: fully dissociated. Weak: partially dissociated.
Strong acids have lower pH, higher conductivity and react faster.
Strength and concentration are different things.

blocks.text: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base. Every neutralisation makes a salt.

blocks.label: Ionic equation for neutralisation
where: This is true for any acid with any alkali.

items: A salt is formed when the H⁺ of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates and nitric acid makes nitrates.
Write full equations with state symbols, then ionic equations by cancelling spectator ions.
Neutralisation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Acid + base makes a salt; carbonates also make CO₂.
The salt name comes from the acid and the base.

blocks.text: A titration finds the exact volume of one solution that reacts with a fixed volume of another. This section covers the method and the calculation.

items.text: Weigh the solid in a weighing bottle. Dissolve it in a beaker with distilled water.
Pour into a volumetric flask. Rinse the beaker and funnel into the flask.
Add water to the mark, with the bottom of the meniscus on the line. Stopper and invert to mix.
Pipette 25.0 cm³ of one solution into a conical flask. Add a few drops of indicator.
Run the other solution in from a burette, swirling, until the indicator just changes colour at the end point.
Do a rough titration first, then repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. Use the mean of the concordant results.
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) = 2.25 × 10⁻³ mol.

diagram.alt: Calculate the concentration of sodium hydroxide from a titration.
diagram.question: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by {v} cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol dm⁻³.
working: Ratio 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) is the same

items: Concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³.
n = c × V for the known solution, then the ratio, then c = n ÷ V.
Check the ratio in the equation; it is not always 1 : 1.

checks.q: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid. Give an example of each.
checks.a: A strong acid is fully dissociated in aqueous solution, e.g. hydrochloric acid. A weak acid is only partially dissociated, e.g. ethanoic acid.

checks.q: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide.
25.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid is neutralised by 30.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.

items: Neutralisation of acids with carbonates, metal oxides and alkalis (water-soluble bases), including full equations.
Explain strong and weak acids qualitatively, in terms of relative dissociation.
Titration calculations may be structured, with steps given, or non-structured. They may use familiar or unfamiliar acids and bases.
Calculate solution concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and g dm⁻³.
Use a range of acids, alkalis and indicators in titrations.
Both phenolphthalein and methyl orange are expected as indicators.
Names and formulae are limited to hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric and ethanoic acids, and sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and ammonia.
Explain the differences between strong and weak acids using a reactive metal, the pH value (pH meter or universal indicator) and conductivity.
